sources.news_title: West Virginia senators oppose resolution limiting president's Iran war powers
sources.text:
West Virginia’s Republican senators, Shelley Moore Capito and Jim Justice, today voted against advancing a joint resolution directing the president to withdraw United States armed forces from Iran unless there’s a declaration of war or authorization to use military force.
The effort to advance the resolution was defeated in a 47-49 vote. One Republican, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, was a yes vote. Senator John Fetterman, a Democrat from Pennsylvania, was a no vote. Two Republican senators who have supported legislation to end the war, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, did not vote.
“I voted no, and the reason I voted no is that the president, I believe, has the right and and the authority to proceed as he has,” Capito said in response to a MetroNews question during a briefing today.
Also today, the House of Representatives passed a war powers resolution in a 214-208 vote. Four Republicans joined Democrats. West Virginia’s Republican representatives, Riley Moore and Carol Miller, were no votes.
The military conflict in Iran has escalated. The United States military has bombed Iran for 12 consecutive nights. The Strait of Hormuz, a major oil supply route, is technically open but commercial traffic has slowed severely because of the ongoing hostilities.
“There is frustration,” Capito said in a briefing with West Virginia reporters. “There’s no doubt about it in terms of the length and sort of the spreading: Now Houthis are involved. Also, the Iranians are bombing six and seven other countries.
“It is morphed into a different type of conflict than what the president originally embarked on to eliminate the possibilities of nuclear weapons. But we have decimated the country in terms of its navy and other things. So I think we’ll continue to have these votes. Votes may change, but as of today, they have not.”
Roughly 500 to 550 U.S. service members have been injured in the conflict. Four U.S. service members have died in the conflict with Iran in recent days. Eighteen American service members are believed to have been killed since the start of the Iran war.
“We saw four service members coming home yesterday, in you know losing their lives in service to our country. Very very young people. Really really sad for them, their families, for the nation. And we want to make sure that we are protecting our troops,” Capito said in comments advocating billions in emergency or supplemental funding to cover the ongoing war in Iran and replace munitions.
Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution assigns Congress the sole and exclusive power to formally declare war. The United States Constitution’s Article II also explicitly designates the president as the commander in chief.
The War Powers Resolution of 1973 restricts the president from committing U.S. troops to armed conflicts without congressional authorization or a declared emergency.
The president may only commit forces for 60 days without congressional approval. The current U.S. fighting with Iran began Feb. 28.
“Now you have to remember that yes, things began in February, but there are have been ceasefires, lulls and everything else, and we have no commitment of troops. So I think that we’re not there yet to be able to tell the president that’s where and how he needs to proceed and he has to come to Congress,” Capito said.
Capito was among the senators who participated in a hearing this week with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Senator Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, asked Hegseth about the War Powers Resolution. “It’s not ambiguous,” she said, noting the start and stop nature of the conflict.
Murkowski asked, “Is the administration still taking that position about needing no authorization from Congress at this time?”
Hegseth responded, “Senator, I know there’s a longstanding legal debate on this particular topic. We certainly as a department share the position of the White House that we share all the authorities necessary at this moment.”
Capito’s chance to ask a question came well into the appropriations hearing. She asked about the rationale for the additional military spending: “What’s the consequence of not passing this supplemental spending?” she asked Caine. “Where do you see that hitting us most deeply?”
Caine responded by saying financial compensation for service members could be strained, also citing operations and maintenance costs plus the ability to make investments toward future capability.
“So not only would it hit us today but it could hit us tomorrow, as well,” Capito responded.
Most observers characterized the Senate hearing as fiery, contentious and tense, even on a bipartisan basis. Hegseth faced aggressive scrutiny from Democratic senators over the administration’s war strategy in Iran and the conflict’s rising cost, and some Republican lawmakers expressed dissatisfaction over a lack of an exit plan.
“The Democrats were pretty harsh in terms of you know, ‘You don’t know what you’re doing and you’re putting our our military in harm’s way,’ and they wanted to make it all about Iran,” Capito said later on “Talk of the Town” on WAJR Radio.
“This is really more about the troops, about the technologies, about the training, about the readiness, about making sure that we are armed, not just for today, but also for the future and our national security.”
Asked a followup question on radio about the state of the war, Capito said, “Iran has no navy. They are very wounded in terms of their missile development, in terms of their ability to get a nuclear weapon, which is the goal of why the president has moved in this direction.
“There is frustration that it has gone on longer than was originally promised, and I share that frustration. I think everybody does, but at the same time, they’ve proven themselves. The Iranians have proven themselves to be what we always knew they were: dishonest terrorists who have hidden and fortified their own country at the peril of their own people to to be able to fund terrorism not just in that region but around the world and kill and try to kill many Americans.”
She concluded, “And so we need to put this to rest. I don’t know how people with a straight face can say ‘Oh they’re stronger than they were when their country has basically been defanged of many of the assets that they had previous to this.'”

sources.news_title: US Senate blocks resolution curbing Trump's Iran war powers
House votes to end Iran war, but Senate Republicans vote to let Trump continue waging it
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The House on Thursday approved a Democratic-led proposal to end the Iran war, directing President Donald Trump to remove armed forces from hostilities.
The resolution is nonbinding, however. The House voted 214-208, with four Republicans joining all Democrats to cast decisive votes for the measure: Reps. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.
Later in the day, the Senate voted 47-49 to reject a “joint resolution” to end the Iran war that would have the force of law, unlike the House version, but would be subject to a presidential veto. One Republican, Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, joined every Democrat except Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania in voting to advance the measure.
Four Republicans didn’t vote: Sens. Katie Britt of Alabama, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky.
The votes in both chambers were pushed by Democrats eager to get Republicans on the record about an unpopular war ahead of the midterm elections and to reassert Congress’ role as the branch of government responsible for declaring war.
Multiple Senate Republicans have said the war should not go on for more than 60 days without congressional approval in order to comply with federal law. They include Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. But both men on Thursday voted against the measure to end the Iran war.
Asked why, Tillis said the 60-day clock started this month, not back in February when Trump and Israel first launched strikes on Iran. “July 10, to my knowledge, is the first time I heard anyone in the administration refer to it as a war,” Tillis said, adding that it would be important for Congress to authorize the war once 60 days are up.
“The clock is ticking. We got to get serious about that,” Tillis said. “I think politically, we can help the president with an unpopular war right now if we provide some legitimacy to it.”
House Republicans have also indicated their willingness to give Trump breathing room on the 60-day deadline. Still, four GOP members voted with Democrats to pass the nonbinding resolution rejecting the war through the Republican-controlled House, reflecting the unpopularity of the conflict.
“The vote today shows that Congress is starting to join the 70% of American people who are against this war, which is clearly a war of choice, and Congress has to step up to our constitutional responsibility and demand it,” Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told NBC News.
Meeks added that Democrats have more tools to force Trump to end the war, such as the “power of the purse” ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline for Congress to fund the government, including the military. He added that he’s introducing a resolution “to sue the administration,” accusing it of defying Congress on the Iran war, which he plans to force a vote on when the House returns from its summer recess in five weeks.
Public opposition to the Iran war has put Republicans in competitive areas in a difficult position.
Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., who represents a swing district and is a top target of Democrats in November, voted against the resolution. He said he recognizes the war’s economic impact but emphasized that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.
“I think people see the prices of fuel and they immediately correlate one and the other. But I think we’re all in agreement that this needs to come to a resolution expeditiously. Under no circumstances should Iran have nuclear weapons,” Bresnahan said Thursday. “Iran is not a friend to the United States, but there needs to be a definitive solution there quickly.”
He said he’d like the Strait of Hormuz to open as soon as possible so the prices of gas and fertilizer can come back down. “The sooner, the better,” he said. “But at the same time, you can’t allow a foreign adversary to run rogue and hold hostage American supply chains because ... they are just acting radically.”
Seven Republicans and two Democrats didn’t cast a vote on the House’s Iran measure Thursday.
It is not the first time that Congress has formally disapproved of the war. The House approved a similar war powers resolution in early June on a 215-208 vote, with the same Republicans supporting it who voted for the measure Thursday. The Senate later passed the same nonbinding measure.
Democrats have continued to force these votes to get Republicans on the record about a war that a majority of Americans oppose. The failed Senate measure was led by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.
“Not only are the vast majority of Americans opposed to this war; it’s the most unpopular war that we’ve had in a very, very, very long time,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said, noting that even self-identified “MAGA” voters are skeptical of the war.
“These are folks who deeply support Donald Trump, but they actually liked when he was talking about ending forever wars instead of getting into them,” she said.

Still, with the Senate weighing its own war powers measure Thursday morning, the move underscores mounting bipartisan unease over a grinding conflict that has recently intensified, including the deaths of four US troops in the region over the weekend, Politico reports.

sources.news_title: House votes to restrain Trump on Iran as Senate rejects similar measure
sources.text:
House votes to limit Trump on Iran; Senate fails to advance similar measure
The votes marked the first test of Republican support for the conflict since President Donald Trump resumed military strikes against Tehran this month.
The House passed a measure to halt the war in Iran on Thursday, as Democrats mounted a last-minute bid to constrain the escalating conflict before lawmakers left Washington for a monthlong recess.
The effort led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D., Wash.) passed by a vote of 214-208. Four Republicans — Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Warren Davidson of Ohio, and Tom Barrett of Michigan — joined Democrats in supporting the measure.
The Senate blocked consideration of a similar resolution hours later on a 49-47 procedural vote.
Sen. Susan Collins of Maine was the lone Republican to join Democrats in supporting the measure. Sen. John Fetterman (D., Pa.) voted against it.
The votes marked the first test of Republican support for the conflict since President Donald Trump resumed strikes against Iran this month. U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, announced it had conducted its 12th consecutive day of airstrikes as Trump pledges to retaliate for the deaths of several American service members killed by Iranian attacks in the last week.
By returning to the war, Trump has forced some vulnerable Republicans into a tenuous political position ahead of the November midterm elections. Iran has closed the Strait of Hormuz — spiking global food and energy markets — and the Houthis, its proxy force in Yemen, have threatened to halt Saudi Arabian oil transiting the Red Sea.
A Washington Post-Ipsos poll earlier this month found that nearly 70% of respondents thought that the war was not “worth fighting.” Eighteen U.S. service members have died during the conflict, with nearly 430 injured.
Earlier this week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers the war will cost about $37.5 billion by the end of September. Congress is debating how to proceed with a $73 billion package to restock the Pentagon’s inventory of precision weapons and cover other costs incurred by the conflict.
“When you’re digging yourself a hole, the first thing you should do is stop digging — and that’s what this resolution seeks to do,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D., Md.), who introduced the resolution, said on the Senate floor before the vote. “Let us stop pretending that Congress has no role to play while American service members remain in harm’s way.”
Sen. Tim Sheehy (R., Mont.), a Navy SEAL veteran who served in Afghanistan and Iraq, countered that passing the resolution would send the wrong message to the U.S. troops fighting the war.
“Think about the people who are deployed right now standing on that wall with a loaded weapon who have volunteered to defend our country and our way of life,” Sheehy said on the Senate floor. “Because they are there defending us in a just war.”
The Trump administration’s return to military strikes in Iran has also divided some Democrats over how best to respond.
The successful vote in the House and the failed one in the Senate came after both chambers approved a separate resolution last month meant to halt the war. Trump has argued the measure lacks the power of law, infuriating Democrats who say the war is being conducted unlawfully without lawmakers’ consent.
The White House has pressured Republicans to oppose such resolutions. Trump complained when he met with Republicans senators last month that the passage of one of the resolutions was undermining his negotiations with the Iranian government.
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R., La.) supported the resolution that passed last month but opposed a subsequent one after being briefed by the White House. He voted against Thursday’s resolution.
Two other Republicans who have voted for similar resolutions in the past, Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska) and Rand Paul of Kentucky), did not vote. Sens. Mitch McConnell (R., Ky.) and Katie Boyd Britt (R., Ala.) also missed the vote.
Rep. Gregory Meeks (D., N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Thursday that he will introduce a resolution to sue the Trump administration over its refusal to abide by their efforts to rein in the war.
Trump “should be coming directly to Congress” to explain why he has continued his war effort in Iran, Meeks said. “Since he’s not, then we should be suing the administration to say ‘You must come to Congress at this point.’”
Sen. Tim Kaine (D., Va.), the architect of Democrats’ strategy to force war powers votes, said he did not think the failed procedural vote in the Senate undercut the successful passage of the war powers resolution last month.
“The substantive vote has been taken,” Kaine said after Thursday’s vote. “Both houses have said, Mr. President, you either have to withdraw troops or” seek authorization from Congress to continue the war.
Still, Kaine said he was turning his attention to pushing back against the war through the appropriations process, through which Congress could exert leverage over the war by refusing to fund it. The House passed a resolution Wednesday taking the first step toward sending $73 billion to the Pentagon and U.S. intelligence agencies, largely to cover the cost of the conflict, but the measure faces an uncertain future in the Senate.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R., S.D.) said the Senate would not take it up immediately as bipartisan negotiations over government funding play out — an approach that some Senate Republicans say is a mistake. The Senate could use the measure to fund the government later if those negotiations collapse.
After the House vote, Rep. Jason Crow (D., Colo.), a co-sponsor of Jayapal’s resolution, said Democrats would continue to force votes on similar resolutions and predicted that more House Republicans would support them after hearing from frustrated constituents while the chamber is on recess over the next four weeks.
“They’re going to get crushed,” Crow told reporters after the vote. “When we come back in September, I bet we have more people joining with us saying, ‘All right, let’s wrap this up.’”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.) signaled that Senate Democrats would also continue to force votes on similar resolutions.
“We will keep forcing votes until Senate Republicans stop playing dumb and summon up the courage to do what is right,” Schumer said on the Senate floor.

sources.news_title: These are the Republicans who voted for the Iran War Powers resolution
House again OKs resolution seeking to halt military action in Iran, but Senate rejects similar one
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The House on Thursday narrowly passed a resolution to halt U.S. military action in Iran, sending a warning to President Donald Trump for the second time as the war has escalated and the future of the conflict is increasingly uncertain.
The 214-208 vote requiring congressional approval for the war came just before the Senate narrowly rejected a similar resolution, 47-49. Though the votes forced by Democrats are largely symbolic, they are meant as a signal to the Republican president that his support on Capitol Hill is chipping away as the war drags on and lawmakers in both parties have questioned his administration’s endgame.
The war has had “no clear mission, no strategy, no end goal,” said Washington Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat who led the resolution on the House floor.
The House resolution passed after a handful of Republicans voted with Democrats to end the war. But the vast majority of Republicans in both chambers voted to back the war and cede congressional war powers to Trump.
Joint U.S. and Israeli airstrikes launched the war in late February. A tenuous ceasefire deal was reached in April, but Trump declared the ceasefire was “over” earlier this month.
Trump has insisted that continued U.S. attacks against Iran do not mean a return to war or long-term action. After the first House vote to halt the war in early June, he posted on social media that it was “unpatriotic” and “meaningless.”
A statement of administration policy issued by the White House on Thursday noted that the resolutions don't have the force of law and encouraged lawmakers to vote against them.
“The President has the Constitutional authority to defend the United States and our citizens from the danger posed by the Iranian regime,” the policy statement said. “This requires the ability to act decisively to ensure it never obtains a nuclear weapon.”
Continued American airstrikes are occurring even as diplomatic efforts show little public sign of progress and officials on both sides have dug in on the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global energy that remains largely closed. The unpopular war threatens further worldwide economic disruption and is sending fuel prices up ahead of midterm U.S. elections this fall.
“We are in this new escalatory phase where Americans have been killed, and Americans are experiencing the rising costs — I think it’s important that people be held accountable,” said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who led the Senate effort on Thursday. “And this is a very unpopular war.”
Most Republicans vote to cede congressional powers
As the House debated the resolution Wednesday evening, Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., read out names of 18 service members killed since the war began.
“To belittle this mission is to belittle and demean the very service these members gave their life for,” Mast said. “Their sacrifice was not meaningless. This operation is bringing reckoning for the hundreds of times Iran has attacked and killed people of the United States of America.”
The top Democrat on the panel, New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, said that presidents are supposed to make the case to Congress.
The service members who died made the ultimate sacrifice for “an illegal unauthorized war that the American people don’t want,” Meeks said.
Democrats said they would continue to force Republicans to vote on the issue.
“If Donald Trump won’t listen to the people and end this war then Congress must,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Trump is watching Iran votes closely
Republicans on both sides of the Capitol know that voting against the war can have a political cost, even as many of them have privately questioned the Trump administration’s handling of the conflict.
In his post after the June House vote, Trump called the four Republicans who voted with Democrats “GRANDSTANDERS!” and said they should be “ashamed of themselves.”
“They would rather have our Country fail than give me another, of many, victories,” he said.
When the Senate passed a war powers resolution on Iran for the first time in June, Trump called the four Republicans who voted for it “losers" and then reprimanded them at a Senate GOP luncheon that he attended the next day.
Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, one of the Republicans who had voted with Democrats, said afterward that he had clashed with Trump over the issue. He said he told Trump directly that he needed to give more details to the public about the conflict.
“This was supposed to last four weeks. It’s lasted four months,” said Cassidy, who had just lost reelection in a primary after Trump endorsed one of his opponents. “Our original objectives have not been achieved.”
Trump argued back, Cassidy later told reporters, and he told the president that he wouldn’t change his vote until he got a briefing. The White House later relented, giving Cassidy a one-on-one meeting, and the Louisiana Republican changed his vote in a late-night do-over vote before the Senate left for a two-week recess.
Cassidy voted against the resolution again on Thursday.
Polling finds Americans disapprove of the war
Most Americans disapprove of the way Trump is handling the situation with Iran, according to recent polling. A Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted in July found that few Americans think the war in Iran has been worth fighting, and most aren’t confident that the U.S. military action in Iran and negotiations to end the war will prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
Only about two-thirds of Republicans approve of Trump’s handling of the situation in Iran, according to the poll. Most Republicans, about 6 in 10, think the war has been worth fighting and are confident that the military action and ensuing negotiations will prevent Iran from development nuclear weapons, but a sizable share — about one-third — are unconvinced.
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said that if Congress can't force Trump to seek congressional authorization then lawmakers should block war funding. The House on Wednesday adopted a Republican-only $95 billion budget proposal, including money for the Iran war, but its future is uncertain in the Senate.
“He wants to break the law, fine, let him break the law, but we control the appropriations process, and that’s what we need to use,” Kaine said.
Associated Press writers Steven Sloan and Amelia Thomson DeVeaux contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Congress splits on war powers resolutions to force Trump to abandon Iran war
sources.text:
Congress on Thursday split on advancing a pair of war powers resolutions aimed at forcing President Donald Trump to abandon his war with Iran, as the conflict escalates into a deadly new phase and oil tops $100 a barrel.
The moves were the first vote since Trump informed Congress that he restarted the war with Iran following the breakdown of peace negotiations. The conflict's revival after weeks of a shaky ceasefire comes just months before the U.S. midterm elections. It threatens to scramble the majority Republicans' plan to maintain their razor-thin majorities.
The Senate on Thursday voted 47-49 to kill a joint resolution under the War Powers Act to force Trump to end hostilities with Iran. That chamber's action follows a 214-208 House vote earlier in the day to approve a similar measure under the War Powers Act.
Even if Congress does try to force Trump to withdraw, he would be almost certain to veto anything that reaches his desk.
"There is no good way out of a bad war," said Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who offered the resolution in the Senate. "This is an opportunity for this Congress to finally take responsibility."
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, voted for the resolution. Collins is locked in a tough reelection bid in a state that is now reliably blue. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the lone Democrat to vote against the measure.
Republicans argued before the vote that cutting off the administration's ability to wage war now would tie their hands.
"If we vote now and Republicans voted to cut and run and force the president in the middle of this to withdraw, it would be a huge blow to American credibility," said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La.
Kennedy downplayed concerns among voters with the war, saying, "I don't think it's the main thing; I think this election will be about the cost of living."

Four House Republicans Break Ranks To Help Democrats Pass Iran War Powers Resolution
The House on Thursday approved a Democratic-led war powers resolution aimed at restricting President Trump's military operations in Iran, with four Republicans providing the decisive votes.
The measure, sponsored by Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and forced to the floor with Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), passed 214-208. Joining every Democrat were Reps. Tom Barrett (R-Mich.), Warren Davidson (R-Ohio), Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) - the same quartet that crossed the aisle on a similar resolution last month.
It will not end the war, or slow it. The measure is a concurrent resolution, meaning it never reaches the president's desk for signature or veto and carries no force of law. Both chambers passed comparable measures in June. The war continued. This one is a message, delivered twice.
The vote comes as the death toll among U.S. service members climbs. Eighteen troops have been killed since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February - four of them since July 17. U.S. forces have sustained nearly 500 injuries, roughly 100 in the past two weeks, according to the Pentagon. On Wednesday, Trump participated in a dignified transfer ceremony for three service members killed in Jordan and Iraq.
Jayapal framed the resolution as a reassertion of congressional authority. "This is a vote of conscience," she said on the House floor Wednesday. "This war must end." Afterward she added: "Congress has not been consulted. And hostilities have been driven over and over again by a president who won his election by promising to end forever wars."
Republicans who opposed the measure defended the campaign as necessary given Iran's record of attacks on Americans in the region. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.) held up photographs of U.S. service members killed in the war during floor debate. "To belittle this mission is to belittle and demean the very service these members gave their life for," Mast said. "This operation is bringing reckoning for the hundreds of times Iran has attacked and killed people of the United States of America."
The four who broke ranks did so for different reasons. Massie and Davidson are longstanding critics of foreign intervention; Fitzpatrick and Barrett are moderates facing competitive re-election bids. Massie suggested the number could grow.
"I think you will see more Republicans come on board to war powers resolutions if we bring them up again, and I'd be happy to vote on one every day, but I don't think we need to," he told CNN on Wednesday evening. "We've already passed a concurrent resolution in the House and in the Senate."
The Senate did not follow. Hours after the House vote, Senate Democrats moved to advance a war powers resolution of their own and fell short, 47-49. In June, GOP Sens. Rand Paul (Ky.), Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Bill Cassidy (La.) had joined Democrats on the earlier measure.
One Bridge Per Ship
The congressional rebuke arrived a day after Trump escalated in the other direction. In a Wednesday Truth Social post, he committed the United States to destroying a piece of Iranian infrastructure for every vessel Iran attacks.
"From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran," Trump wrote.
Tehran answered within hours. An Iranian military source told the semi-official Tasnim News Agency that if the United States targets a bridge or power plant in Iran, Iran will "strike infrastructure and bridges in the region, including energy facilities where the United States has interests." The source restated Tehran's position that ships may transit the strait safely only if coordinated with Iran and conducted under Iranian arrangements.
U.S. Central Command says Iran has attacked more than 30 commercial vessels in the strait over the past three months, and the U.S. had completed 11 consecutive nights of strikes on Iranian military infrastructure as of Wednesday. Several of those Iranian attacks came after Washington and Tehran signed a June memorandum of understanding calling for a ceasefire - an agreement the administration says Iran has violated. Qatari mediators are still working toward a deal that would stop the fighting and reopen the waterway.
The House action underscores persistent bipartisan unease with the trajectory of the conflict, even as the White House signals a willingness to escalate. Two chambers have now told the president to stop, twice, in language he is free to ignore.

Four House Republicans broke with President Donald Trump and most of their party on Thursday, voting with Democrats to pass a resolution seeking to halt U.S. military action in Iran unless Congress provides explicit authorization.
Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Tom Barrett of Michigan and Thomas Massie of Kentucky joined Democrats in backing the House measure, which passed the chamber 214-208. The same four Republicans voted against Trump's Iran war powers in June.
Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican, supported a similar resolution in the upper chamber later Thursday. The measure ultimately did not pass the Senate, 47-49.

The 1973 War Powers Resolution allows Congress to direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from hostilities not authorized by lawmakers. Presidents of both parties have challenged limits on executive war powers, but the law remains one of Congress’ primary checks on unilateral military action.
It also requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing U.S. forces into hostilities and limits unauthorized military action to 60 days.
Trump did not seek congressional authorization before launching military strikes against Iran in February, and many Democrats argued the action was unconstitutional. Republican Reps. Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Thomas Massie of Kentucky split from their party to vote in favor of the resolution.

Jason Crow of Colorado wrote in a letter to their Democratic colleagues ahead of the vote.

The votes came amid an escalation of the renewed conflict after a recent ceasefire came to an end. This was the second time the House has voted to check the president’s ability to continue waging war, but the first after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran collapsed.
Democrats have repeatedly forced votes to limit Trump’s war powers in both the House and the Senate, but the campaign has gradually picked up more GOP support in a sign of growing discontent within the party over the ongoing conflict.
The bodies of four American service members killed during the Iran war returned to the United States in flag-draped cases on Wednesday.
Some Democrats who champion the war powers efforts have argued that the concurrent resolutions are still legally binding, and argue the courts have not ruled on whether they lack legal effect when dealing with war powers measures.
House Democrats emphasized on Thursday that they are making a politically popular choice in voting repeatedly to rein in President Donald Trump’s authorities in Iran as the war drags on ahead of the midterm elections.
“I think that Americans of all backgrounds are sick of seeing the United States enter wars without justification, spending trillions of dollars in our engagements abroad,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told reporters.
The New York progressive said the passage of the war powers measure before the House left for August recess sends a message “of both the depravity and wrongheadedness of going into Iran, offending the global economy, and also a complete lack of focus on the needs of working class American.”
The resolution’s sponsor, Rep. Pramila Jayapal, said she believes Republicans who did not show up to vote “did not want to take a ‘no’ vote, and then have to go home to their constituents and explain to them why they voted ‘no’ on ending this illegal war instead of focusing on what Americans really want to focus on.”
The president has sharply criticized Republicans for voting for to advance previous war powers resolutions, chastising them in closed-door meetings and posting on Truth Social that they are “losers” who “made my job more difficult.”
In June, during the ceasefire, the Senate adopted a resolution aimed at removing military forces from Iran, though the chamber walked back the rebuke a day later when they failed to advance a similar war powers measure.

Trump defends Iran war after lawmakers split on supporting conflict
President Donald Trump defended his administration's ongoing war with Iran after four U.S. troops were killed over the weekend and hours after the House and Senate split on whether to tell the president to end the conflict.
"We want to get it over with, and we want to do it right, but we have to... do what we came to do," Trump said Thursday afternoon.
Earlier Thursday, the House of Representatives voted to end the war 214-208, with four Republicans joining Democrats to rebuke the White House. The Senate then struck down a similar measure, with key Republicans backing the president.
The resolutions were largely symbolic and would not have forced an end to the war, but did force lawmakers to record their stance less than four months before most of them face re-election. More than two-thirds of Americans said they disapprove of Trump's handling of the Iran war in a Washington Post/Ipsos poll earlier this month.
The vote comes two days after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asked Congress for $67 billion in additional funding for the war, prompting Democrats to question whether the administration has a plan to end the war. Iran and the United States continue to fight over control of the Strait of Hormuz as Tehran has periodically attacked ships in order to deter traffic and choke the world's oil supply, prompting increased volatility in already high gasoline prices.
Trump on Iran war: 'We have to do what we came to do'
Francesca Chambers
Trump defended his administration's ongoing military campaign hours after the House voted to end the war with Iran, while the Senate sided with the president.
"We want to get it over with, and we want to do it right, but we have to... do what we came to do," Trump said at an event at the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington, DC. "We can't let them have what they want, which is nuclear weapons."
Trump's remarks came a day after he attended the dignified transfer of four U.S. service members who were killed in overseas fighting related to the conflict. "I had a very sad day yesterday," Trump said Thursday, July 23.
A total of 18 Americans have been killed since the war began on Feb. 28.
Comparing the death toll to previous wars in which thousands of lives were lost, Trump added: "One is too many, but it's 18."
Saudi Arabia gets nuclear deal. Iran gets bombed. What's in the pact?
Kim Hjelmgaard
The Trump administration signed an agreement with Saudi Arabia to develop a nuclear program, even as the White House escalates a war with Iran that is aimed, in part, at destroying its nuclear capabilities.
The U.S. Department of Energy described the agreement as one that would allow Saudi Arabia to develop its civilian energy nuclear program and give U.S. companies "great access" to related commercial deals.
Congress has not yet approved the arrangement, and few details about it have been made public. But former officials and members of the nuclear community said it is a major shift in U.S. policy and risks accelerating a nuclear arms race in an already volatile region.
The deal is designed to give U.S. companies a key role in developing Saudi Arabia’s nuclear infrastructure. This stands in stark contrast to the war being waged by the Trump administration to halt Iran's nuclear program.
Like Saudi Arabia, Iran insists – despite significant international skepticism – that it is only interested in nuclear energy, not nuclear weapons. But Saudi Arabia and Iran are historic rivals who compete for regional dominance.
GOP defectors have differing motives
Phillip M. Bailey
The four Republicans who sided with House Democrats on ending the war with Iran have varying political motivations and relationships with President Trump.
Both Fitzpatrick and Barrett are running for reelection in swing districts in Pennsylvania and Michigan respectively, which the GOP need to hold if they hope to keep their razor-thin House majority.
Democrats have focused much of their messaging around rising gas prices in both of their districts ahead of the 2026 midterms, particularly in Fitzpatrick's area which covers Philadelphia suburbs in the southeastern corner of the Keystone State.
The average cost to fill up has climbed to about $4.23 a gallon in the state, according to AAA, which is $1 higher than a year ago.
Massie is among a group of so-called "free agents" in Washington who've lost their primaries after clashing with the president, but remain in Congress.
Davidson, however, is a bit of an outlier. He's representing an Ohio seat that rated as "safe" by experts but he has criticized the war without facing Trump's wrath.
"For some, this debate will be about whether we should even be fighting in Iran," Davidson said on the House floor in March. "For me, the debate is more fundamental: Is the president of the United States, regardless of the person holding the office, empowered to do whatever he wants? That's not what our Constitution says."
Tillis a 'no' on ending war — for now
Zachary Schermele
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, told USA TODAY that although he voted "no" on Thursday’s war powers resolution, he will flip his vote and support ending hostilities after Sept. 10.
His rationale: That is 60 days from what he says is the first time the Trump administration referred to the conflict as a war.
The War Powers Act gives the president a 60-day window to receive authorization to officially declare a war from Congress — which technically has that specific power under the Constitution.
Senate rejects war powers resolution
Erin Mansfield
The Senate voted down a measure that would have directed the president to end the war in Iran, just hours after the House passed a similar measure led by Democrats.
The measure failed 49-47.
The measure is largely symbolic but required senators facing re-election Nov. 7 to take a public stance on the war.
Senate votes on Iran war
Erin Mansfield and Zachary Schermele
A vote is underway in the Senate over whether to direct President Donald Trump to remove U.S. service members from Iran.
The measure appears likely to fail because prominent Republican critics of Trump, including Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, voted against it.
House Democrats celebrate war powers vote
Zachary Schermele
On the steps of the Capitol, Democrats took a victory lap after the House again rebuked the war.
“We’re thrilled with this vote tally,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Washington.
Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colorado, said accountability was “coming back to life” in Congress.
“What you just saw was the United States Congress doing its job, to take an up or down vote on matters of war and peace,” he said.
House already passed defense spending
Erin Mansfield
The House of Representatives on July 22 passed a $1.15 trillion military spending bill by a margin of 216-212, with Republicans largely in support and Democrats largely opposed.
Seven Republican lawmakers, however, bucked the White House and voted against the package. Six Democrats voted in favor.
Every year, the House and Senate each pass their own versions of the annual military spending bill and then negotiate a compromise before sending it to the president for his signature.
Contributing: Reuters
House votes to end Iran war
Zachary Schermele
The House voted again Thursday to end military hostilities in Iran, with four Republicans bucking the White House.
The measure passed 214-208.
The GOP lawmakers were Reps. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Tom Barrett of Michigan.
Rubio says Houthis were 'suckered' into attacks
Erin Mansfield
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that Iran pulled the Houthis into bombing ships in the Red Sea overnight, and hoped they would change their behavior and stay out of the conflict with Iran.
"They got suckered into this by the Iranians," Rubio said during a trip to Southeast Asia. "The Houthis largely were smart and stayed out of this throughout the conflict, but now the apparently have gotten themselves suckered into this going after Saudi Arabia and their ships."
Rubio pointed to reports overnight of Saudi ships carrying 4 million barrels of oil for China that were attempting to exit the Red Sea.
"Are they going to blow up the Chinese ship and this becomes a problem for China?" Rubio asked. "This will become a problem for the whole world. But I hope that they will de-escalate."
U.S. Air Force deploys B-1 bomber to strike Iran targets
Natalie Neysa Alund
The United States deployed a B-1 long-range bomber to strike targets in Iran since the renewal of the conflict between the countries less than two weeks ago, according to multiple news outlets.
The supersonic plane, part of the U.S. Air Force's military bomber fleet, carries up to 2,000 pounds of bombs and can reach speeds up to Mach 1.2, according to according to information from the Air Force Global Strike Command.
According to The Jerusalem Post, the military deployed the B-1 on Tuesday, July 21, and struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets.
It was not immediately known what targets were struck but Axios reported the long-range bomber launched its mission from an airbase in the UK and was spotted on online plane tracking websites.
As of Thursday, July 23, CENTCOM had not publicly released information about Tuesday's strike or said whether any casualties were involved.
Global oil price returns to $100 per barrel, gas prices likely to rise again
Rachel Barber
Oil prices surged Thursday morning after Iran-backed Houthi militants said they attacked two oil tankers from Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally, in the Red Sea. The group controls the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a waterway that has been used as an alternative oil shipping route as U.S.-Iran hostilities limited traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude oil — the international benchmark — rose more than 6% on Thursday, returning to $100 per barrel and its highest level since late May. West Texas Intermediate oil — the U.S. benchmark — rose 5% to near $91 per barrel, its highest level since early June.
Gas prices, which often lag oil prices, remain above $4 per gallon. As of Thursday morning, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is $4.09, up from $3.93 last month and $3.16 this time last year.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in an X post Thursday that the national average could climb to somewhere between $4.25 and $4.40 per gallon “in the next couple weeks.”

sources.news_title: Resolution calling on Trump to end Iran war approved in House
sources.text:
Congress splits on two war powers resolution votes
Four House Republicans join Democrats for the second time in supporting a halt to the hostilities
The House and Senate, in votes Thursday on ending the Iran war, came to different conclusions, but the majority of voting members of Congress said it is time to bring U.S. troops home.
The House, for the second time, formally called on President Donald Trump to end the war, approving 214-208 a nonbinding concurrent resolution (H Con Res 89) by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash.
The Senate, in an 47-49 vote, fell just short of discharging from the Foreign Relations Committee a binding joint resolution (S J Res 180) by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., that would halt U.S. involvement in the conflict.
Despite the conflicting results, the votes indicate that political pressure on Trump to find a way out of the war is at a minimum not decreasing, as the conflict itself has flared in recent weeks and may widen further.
In the Senate vote, Democrats and Republicans mostly stuck together as usual, with a few exceptions on either side.
Two GOP members who have at least once previously supported an Iran war powers resolution were absent on Thursday: Sens. Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska. Also not voting were two Republican senators who have previously opposed similar resolutions: Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky and Katie Britt of Alabama.
Sen. Susan Collins of Maine once again split with the majority of Republicans and voted for Van Hollen’s resolution.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who has voted both for and against war powers resolutions, voted no on Thursday, later telling reporters he thought the resolution would trigger an “immediate” withdrawal that would not be “reasonable.” And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., continued his pattern of defecting from the Democrat position with another vote opposing an Iran war powers resolution.
“This is a strategic blunder on a massive scale,” Van Hollen said of the war in floor remarks ahead of the vote. “It’s a self-inflicted wound on our country. And for what?”
In the House, meanwhile, as with previous war powers votes, GOP Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Tom Barrett of Michigan voted with Democrats to push the resolution into adoption.
Congress already adopted a similar resolution last month. But as a concurrent resolution, it did not go to the president for his signature and therefore had little power to actually force him to withdraw troops from the war.
Upping the pressure
Democrats maintain the repeated votes serve a purpose — to force Republicans to go on the record about a politically unpopular war amid mounting casualties and to send a message to Trump that Congress is fed up.
“We’re going to keep the pressure on our Republican colleagues,” said Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., in a floor speech before the vote. “It’s Congress that has the power to bring war and so it is perfectly appropriate and right and part of our obligation as the opposition party to force our Republican colleagues to vote again and again and again until they see the light.”
Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told reporters after the vote that there are multiple goals in holding the votes.
“The main goal is we want to end this war, stop spending this money, stop putting our servicemembers’ lives at risk,” Crow said. “But we also have different goals, and that is to hold people accountable who have turned their back on their duty and on the Constitution and on their constituents, and not allowing them to hide.”
Later Thursday, Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced a resolution that would, if adopted, allow him to file a lawsuit to enforce the war powers resolution Congress previously adopted. Specifically, it would require Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to serve as the lead plaintiff in a lawsuit, which a release from Meeks’ office said would address concerns about legal standing.
Previewing the new resolution Thursday morning, Meeks told reporters he plans to try to force a vote on it once the House returns from its summer recess.
“I’m going to force a vote on that so that we can now go to the courts and sue the administration for not following the will of Congress,” Meeks said.
Mideast escalation
The latest vote comes as the war heats up again after a lull in fighting while the Trump administration negotiated with Iran on a framework for further negotiations to end the war.
Last month, the Trump administration announced it had reached a memorandum of understanding with Iran. But less than a month later, Trump declared the MOU “over.” On July 10, he formally notified Congress fighting in the war had resumed.
Over the weekend, three U.S. troops were killed in an Iranian attack on a base in Jordan, while a fourth U.S. service member in Iraq died during what was supposed to be a controlled detonation of an unexploded Iranian drone.
Iran’s proxy group in Yemen, the Houthis, struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea on Wednesday. Such attacks could choke off another bottleneck in the global economy in addition to the ongoing throttling of trade in the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the war.
Apparently in response, the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil exceeded $100 on Thursday for the first time since May.
The national average price of a gallon of gas in the United States averaged just over $4 on Thursday, per AAA. And polls show the war is unpopular among Americans.
Trump has responded with escalating threats, posting on Truth Social on Thursday that “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves” should the Houthis continue attacking ships.
U.S. forces have also conducted 12 consecutive nights of strikes against Iran, with U.S. Central Command saying Wednesday that night’s strikes targeted “maritime capabilities, missile and drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and air defense assets.”
Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: House again passes resolution seeking to halt military action in Iran
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The House on Thursday narrowly passed a resolution to halt U.S. military action in Iran, sending a warning to President Donald Trump for the second time as the war has escalated and the future of the conflict is increasingly uncertain.
The 214-208 vote requiring congressional approval for the war came just before the Senate narrowly rejected a similar resolution, 47-49. Though the votes forced by Democrats are largely symbolic, they are meant as a signal to the Republican president that his support on Capitol Hill is chipping away as the war drags on and lawmakers in both parties have questioned his administration's endgame.
The war has had "no clear mission, no strategy, no end goal," said Washington Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat who led the resolution on the House floor.
The House resolution passed after a handful of Republicans voted with Democrats to end the war. But the vast majority of Republicans in both chambers voted to back the war and cede congressional war powers to Trump.
Joint U.S. and Israeli airstrikes launched the war in late February. A tenuous ceasefire deal was reached in April, but Trump declared the ceasefire was "over" earlier this month.
Trump has insisted that continued U.S. attacks against Iran do not mean a return to war or long-term action. After the first House vote to halt the war in early June, he posted on social media that it was "unpatriotic" and "meaningless."
A statement of administration policy issued by the White House on Thursday noted that the resolutions don't have the force of law and encouraged lawmakers to vote against them.
"The President has the Constitutional authority to defend the United States and our citizens from the danger posed by the Iranian regime," the policy statement said. "This requires the ability to act decisively to ensure it never obtains a nuclear weapon."
Continued American airstrikes are occurring even as diplomatic efforts show little public sign of progress and officials on both sides have dug in on the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global energy that remains largely closed. The unpopular war threatens further worldwide economic disruption and is sending fuel prices up ahead of midterm U.S. elections this fall.
"We are in this new escalatory phase where Americans have been killed, and Americans are experiencing the rising costs — I think it's important that people be held accountable," said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who led the Senate effort on Thursday. "And this is a very unpopular war."
As the House debated the resolution Wednesday evening, Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., read out names of 18 service members killed since the war began.
"To belittle this mission is to belittle and demean the very service these members gave their life for," Mast said. "Their sacrifice was not meaningless. This operation is bringing reckoning for the hundreds of times Iran has attacked and killed people of the United States of America."
The top Democrat on the panel, New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, said that presidents are supposed to make the case to Congress.
The service members who died made the ultimate sacrifice for "an illegal unauthorized war that the American people don't want," Meeks said.
Democrats said they would continue to force Republicans to vote on the issue.
"If Donald Trump won't listen to the people and end this war then Congress must," said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Republicans on both sides of the Capitol know that voting against the war can have a political cost, even as many of them have privately questioned the Trump administration's handling of the conflict.
In his post after the June House vote, Trump called the four Republicans who voted with Democrats "GRANDSTANDERS!" and said they should be "ashamed of themselves."
"They would rather have our Country fail than give me another, of many, victories," he said.
When the Senate passed a war powers resolution on Iran for the first time in June, Trump called the four Republicans who voted for it "losers" and then reprimanded them at a Senate GOP luncheon that he attended the next day.
Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, one of the Republicans who had voted with Democrats, said afterward that he had clashed with Trump over the issue. He said he told Trump directly that he needed to give more details to the public about the conflict.
"This was supposed to last four weeks. It's lasted four months," said Cassidy, who had just lost reelection in a primary after Trump endorsed one of his opponents. "Our original objectives have not been achieved."
Trump argued back, Cassidy later told reporters, and he told the president that he wouldn't change his vote until he got a briefing. The White House later relented, giving Cassidy a one-on-one meeting, and the Louisiana Republican changed his vote in a late-night do-over vote before the Senate left for a two-week recess.
Cassidy voted against the resolution again on Thursday.
Most Americans disapprove of the way Trump is handling the situation with Iran, according to recent polling. A Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted in July found that few Americans think the war in Iran has been worth fighting, and most aren't confident that the U.S. military action in Iran and negotiations to end the war will prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
Only about two-thirds of Republicans approve of Trump's handling of the situation in Iran, according to the poll. Most Republicans, about 6 in 10, think the war has been worth fighting and are confident that the military action and ensuing negotiations will prevent Iran from development nuclear weapons, but a sizable share — about one-third — are unconvinced.
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said that if Congress can't force Trump to seek congressional authorization then lawmakers should block war funding. The House on Wednesday adopted a Republican-only $95 billion budget proposal, including money for the Iran war, but its future is uncertain in the Senate.

sources.text:
The U.S. House passed a resolution directing President Donald Trump to end hostilities with Iran in a largely symbolic vote, as Trump is not expected to sign legislation limiting his own authority.
The resolution passed 214-208, with four Republicans joining Democrats in support. An effort in the Republican-held Senate to advance a similar bill failed hours later. The Senate's vote is a likely indication that the House's resolution will likely die before reaching the Senate floor.
The bill would require the president to withdraw U.S. troops from hostile actions against Iran and its government unless Congress authorizes the use of military force. The measure states it is not intended to prevent the military from defending against an imminent attack.
The resolution has become a politically difficult issue for Republicans, who are balancing support for the White House with concerns about the war’s effect on gas and oil prices. On Thursday, Brent crude oil prices rose above $100 a barrel. The U.S. also has seen higher gas and energy prices in the months since the conflict began.

The debate also has renewed questions about Congress’ authority over military action.
Under the War Powers Resolution, the president must notify Congress within 48 hours of initiating military action. The law allows U.S. forces to remain engaged for up to 60 days without congressional authorization.
However, multiple presidential administrations have conducted military operations without explicit approval from Congress.
Thursday’s resolution came less than a day after the House passed a $95 billion spending bill that included $60 billion for the Pentagon. Democrats opposed the measure as they sought to limit President Donald Trump’s ability to engage militarily with Iran.

sources.text:
By Patricia Zengerle
WASHINGTON, July 23 (Reuters) – The Republican-led U.S. House of Representatives backed a resolution on Thursday directing President Donald Trump to halt U.S. military action against Iran unless he obtains Congress’ approval, but the Senate voted hours later to block a separate, similar measure.
The House vote, the latest rebuke of Trump from Congress, was 214-208 in favor of the war powers resolution as four Republicans joined Democrats in voting for it.
But the Senate voted 49 to 47 to block its own war powers measure within hours of the House vote.
The House resolution, introduced by Representative Pramila Jayapal, a Washington Democrat, directed Trump “to remove the use of United States Armed Forces from hostilities” against Iran unless Congress authorizes it. However, it was largely symbolic. Lawmakers have passed similar resolutions repeatedly in recent months, but they have not led to a cessation of the war.
The four House Republicans who voted in favor were Tom Barrett of Michigan, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Thomas Massie of Kentucky.
In the Senate procedural vote, Republican Susan Collins of Maine voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution and Democrat John Fetterman of Pennsylvania voted with Republicans against it. Four Senators did not vote.
Trump’s Republicans hold slim majorities in the House and Senate.
The votes reflected growing frustration among lawmakers of both parties about a conflict that Trump pitched as a quick, focused effort that would trigger Iran‘s capitulation but instead has become a morass for the United States.
Trump recently announced a ramp-up in attacks on Iran, and the deaths of more U.S. service members. Trump on Thursday promised “major military punishment” for Iran and its Houthi allies, after the Yemeni fighters struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint.
Additionally, two weeks since the effective collapse of an interim truce meant to end the war, the U.S. military launched another nightly round of airstrikes on Iran, prompting Iran to fire at U.S. bases in neighboring countries.
(Reporting by Patricia Zengerle, Editing by Rod Nickel and Don Durfee)
